analysis.one_liner: Places a moratorium on government facial recognition use until a commission sets rules.
analysis.headline: The bill never advanced past its committee referral; the Senate Homeland Security Committee took no action before the Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would bar federal officials from using facial recognition to identify people without a warrant, and would block federal dollars from funding state and local facial recognition systems, until a 13-member congressional commission writes rules for both government and commercial use of the technology. People harmed by violations could sue in federal court. The commission would have to include a majority of members representing communities most affected by the technology.
analysis.who_benefits: If passed, the bill would protect everyone from warrantless government face-scanning, with its findings singling out communities of color, activists, immigrants, and other groups it says are disproportionately misidentified or targeted [S3]. Federal, state, and local police would lose the ability to run identification searches without a warrant, and people whose faces were scanned unlawfully could go to court to stop it [S2].

how_it_helps.text: Bars any federal official or contractor from setting up facial recognition cameras, using data from the technology, or importing it to identify people in the U.S. without a warrant until Congress enacts rules built on the commission's guidelines [S2] [S3].

Prohibits the use of federal funds by state or local governments to buy facial recognition software, services, or images, cutting off a pipeline of federal money into local surveillance systems [S2] [S3].
Lets any aggrieved person sue a federal official in U.S. district court for an injunction or a declaration that the ban was violated [S2] [S3].

Creates a commission where at least 7 of 13 members must represent communities most negatively affected by facial recognition, and directs it to write rules guarding against a 'constant state of surveillance,' biased results, and discrimination [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Law enforcement agencies would lose a warrantless identification tool, and facial recognition vendors would lose a government market that the bill's findings describe as actively marketed to police departments across the country [S3]. The commission is also directed to preserve law enforcement's ability to track missing and exploited children and trafficked people [S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Police agencies and facial recognition vendors

drawbacks.text: A blanket moratorium could impede legitimate law enforcement work; the bill itself directs the commission to preserve the ability to find missing and exploited children and trafficked individuals, an acknowledgment that the technology has some rescue-oriented uses [S3].

The warrant requirement leaves room for continued government use once a judge signs a warrant, so the protection is not a total ban, and critics of restrictions could argue the warrant exception is too permissive [S3].
The bill only restricts government use pending the commission; commercial facial recognition companies would face no direct limits until a later Congress enacted implementing legislation [S2] [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The main benefit is stopping warrantless government face-scanning while rules are written, which matters most to the communities the bill says are misidentified most often. The cost is real but narrower: law enforcement loses a warrantless tool that could help find missing children or trafficking victims, which the bill tries to address by requiring the commission to protect those uses. The design leans on a commission and future legislation rather than a permanent ban, so its protections would only be as strong as what Congress later enacts.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in February 2020, read twice, and referred to the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee, which took no further action before the Congress ended in January 2021 [S1] [S5].

narrative.text: Sen. Merkley introduced the bill on February 12, 2020, joined by Sen. Booker as its sole cosponsor [S1] [S3] [S4].
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs, and the action history records no hearing, markup, or vote afterward [S5].
The 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021 with the bill still sitting in committee, so it died there [S1] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Police agencies and facial recognition vendors are better off because the moratorium never passed, since warrantless government use and public procurement of the technology continued unchanged; the communities the bill said were disproportionately targeted remain without the federal limits it proposed.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Police agencies and surveillance tech vendors

for.name: Sen. Jeff Merkley
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Ethical Use of Facial Recognition Act in the Senate.

against.name: Sen. Ron Johnson
against.role: Chair, Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee
against.what_they_did: His committee received the bill by referral and never scheduled a hearing or markup, leaving it to die at the end of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken; the bill's only two supporters were Democrats and it stalled in a Republican-chaired committee without any recorded opposition vote.

industries.industry: Facial recognition and surveillance technology vendors
industries.note: The bill would cut these companies off from federal procurement and from federal grants that state and local governments use to buy their systems. The bill's findings describe the technology as actively marketed to law enforcement nationwide, and its accuracy failures fall on the ordinary people being misidentified.

industries.industry: Federal, state, and local law enforcement
industries.note: Police would lose the ability to identify people by face without a warrant, but the commission's mandate requires preserving their ability to find missing and exploited children and trafficking victims. Some agencies lose a tool they currently use without court approval.
